question: Will the Fed increase interest rates by 25 bps after the September 2026 meeting?
description:
The FED interest rates are defined in this market by the upper bound of the target federal funds range. The decisions on the target federal funds range are made by the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meetings.

This market will resolve to the amount of basis points the upper bound of the target federal funds rate is changed by versus the level it was prior to the Federal Reserve's September 2026 meeting.

If the target federal funds rate is changed to a level not expressed in the displayed options, the change will be rounded up to the nearest 25 and will resolve to the relevant bracket. (e.g. if there's a cut/increase of 12.5 bps it will be considered to be 25 bps)

The resolution source for this market is the FOMC’s statement after its meeting scheduled for September 15-16, 2026 according to the official calendar: https://www.federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/fomccalendars.htm.

The level and change of the target federal funds rate is also published at the official website of the Federal Reserve at https://www.federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/openmarket.htm.

This market may resolve as soon as the FOMC’s statement for their September meeting with relevant data is issued. If no statement is released by the end date of the next scheduled meeting, this market will resolve to the "No change" bracket.

eventMetadata.context_description:
**Persistent inflation above the Fed’s 2% target, driven largely by energy and supply shocks tied to geopolitical tensions, remains the dominant driver behind the 68.5% probability of no change at the September 15-16 FOMC meeting.** Recent PCE readings near 3.7% year-over-year and core measures around 3.3-3.4% have kept pressure on policymakers, reinforced by Chair Kevin Warsh’s emphasis on restoring price stability after the July 28-29 decision to hold the federal funds rate at 3.50%-3.75% (9-3 vote with three dissents favoring a hike).

The 30.5% odds of a 25-basis-point increase reflect ongoing trader focus on inflation credibility and the hawkish tilt in the June dot plot, where nine participants projected at least one hike by year-end. However, the labor market’s relative stability—unemployment near 4.1-4.2% with moderate wage growth around 3.5%—has reduced the urgency for immediate tightening, supporting the higher probability of a hold. Cut probabilities stay negligible (under 2% combined) amid the absence of clear disinflationary momentum.

Incoming July and August inflation and employment data will determine whether probabilities shift before the meeting, with markets currently pricing a modest but meaningful chance of action only if readings reaccelerate.
